An audition is a live tryout — a short performance or demonstration that someone gives in front of a person (or a group of people) who are evaluating whether that person is the right fit for a role, a position, or an opportunity in a performance-based field.
The core idea

Imagine a theater company is putting on a play and needs an actor to play the lead character. They can't just pick someone randomly, nor is a written application enough — they need to see and hear what each person can actually do. So they invite people to come in and perform, one by one. Each of those individual tryout sessions is called an audition.

The word captures a specific kind of evaluation: one where skill, talent, or suitability must be demonstrated live, in person, in real time.
Where auditions happen

Auditions are used anywhere a selection must be made based on live performance. Some examples:

  • A film director holds auditions to find the right actor for a role in a movie
  • A music school holds auditions to decide who gets admitted
  • A symphony orchestra holds auditions to hire a new violinist or cellist
  • A dance company holds auditions to choose performers for a production
  • A TV talent competition (like American Idol or The Voice) holds auditions to pick its contestants
  • A theater group holds auditions to cast all the different parts in a play

The defining feature is always the same: you can't just be chosen based on your reputation or a piece of paper — you have to come in and show the selectors what you can do, live.
What actually happens during an audition

The person auditioning comes prepared with something to perform. Depending on the context, this might be:

  • A monologue (a prepared speech or scene from a play or film, performed solo)
  • A song (performed live, sometimes with or without musical accompaniment)
  • A dance routine
  • A piece played on a musical instrument

After this prepared portion, the selectors may also ask the person to do something unexpected on the spot. For example, they might hand them a script they have never seen before and ask them to read it aloud immediately — this is called a cold reading, and it tests how naturally and quickly someone can perform under pressure.

Throughout all of this, the selectors are watching carefully, listening, and forming judgments.
What selectors are looking for

The people conducting the audition aren't just looking for the most technically skilled person. They are usually looking for a combination of things:

  • Raw talent and skill in the relevant discipline
  • How well the person fits the specific role — their look, voice, energy, or presence
  • How the person handles pressure and unexpected directions
  • A certain quality or feeling that's hard to describe but easy to recognize — sometimes called "it factor" or "star quality"
  • In ensemble productions (like a band or a dance company), whether the person fits in with the rest of the group

This is why auditions can feel unpredictable — two equally talented people can audition for the same role, and the selectors will choose the one who simply felt more right for that particular project.
Who the selectors are

Depending on the context, the people judging an audition might be:

  • A casting director (in film and TV, this is a specialist whose entire job is to find actors for roles)
  • A director of a play or film
  • A panel of judges (in talent competitions or school admissions)
  • A conductor (for an orchestra)
  • A choreographer (for dance)
  • A panel of faculty (for a music or performing arts school)

Sometimes it's one person sitting alone in a room; other times it's a whole panel of people, which can feel even more intimidating.
Types of auditions

Open audition (also known as a "cattle call")
Anyone is welcome to show up and audition, with no invitation required. These are common for large productions and can draw hundreds of hopeful performers. The term "cattle call" (a casual, slightly irreverent nickname) reflects the sheer volume of people that can show up.

Closed or invited audition
Only people who have been specifically contacted and invited are allowed to audition. These are more selective and often used for higher-profile or more specialized roles.

Callback
After the first round of auditions, the selectors narrow down the pool and invite their top candidates back for a second (or even third) audition. This follow-up is called a callback. Getting a callback is a very positive sign — it means the selectors are seriously considering you. The final decision is often made after one or more callbacks.

Screen test
Used primarily in film and TV, a screen test is when the candidate is filmed on camera — not just to see how they perform, but to evaluate how they appear specifically on screen, which can look very different from how someone appears in person. Screen tests sometimes involve performing scenes with other actors being considered for related roles.
The emotional experience of an audition

Auditions are famously nerve-wracking. You are being observed and judged, often in a cold or unfamiliar room, in front of strangers, often knowing that many other people are competing for the same spot. The pressure is real and the stakes can feel enormous.

This is why the word "audition" often carries a kind of emotional weight. When people talk about going to an audition, there's an implied sense of vulnerability — you are exposing your talent and being evaluated, knowing that rejection is a very real possibility.

The outcome is almost always one of two things:

  • You are selected — you "got the part," "got the role," or "passed the audition"
  • You are not selected — you were "passed over," "didn't make it," or were simply "not right for the role this time"

Rejection at an audition is an extremely common experience, even for very talented people. Professional performers often audition dozens or hundreds of times before landing a role.
A rarer, more technical meaning

In older or more formal academic and medical writing, "audition" can simply mean the sense of hearing or the act of hearing — as in, "the organ responsible for audition is the ear." This usage is not common in everyday speech today, and when you encounter the word in modern conversation or writing, it almost always refers to the performance tryout described throughout this explanation.
Metaphorical use in everyday speech

People sometimes borrow the word "audition" informally to describe any situation where someone is being sized up or tested, even outside of the arts. For example:

  • "This first date feels like an audition."
  • "That presentation was basically her audition for the promotion."

In these cases, the speaker isn't being literal — they're using "audition" to suggest that someone is being watched and evaluated, drawing on the competitive and high-stakes feeling that auditions naturally carry.
The short version

An audition is a live performance-based tryout where someone demonstrates their talent or skill in front of selectors who will decide whether to cast, hire, or admit them. It is competitive, evaluative, and central to the worlds of acting, music, dance, and the performing arts broadly.
